en: The Fourth Chapter of the *Siddhaikavīratantra* (RBTS 20)

Oṃ! You are salt-water, you are sharp, you are fierce, you are terrifying. Burn the limbs of [Name], burn his flesh, burn his skin; burn even his nails, burn his bones, and from the bones, burn the marrow.
Salt dissolves, salt breaks, salt cooks; when the salt of the earth is being carried away, whence can there be sleep? Whence can there be pleasure?
Even if he dwells a hundred yojanas away, or across a hundred rivers,
or within a city surrounded by iron walls and infested with black serpents—
bring him under your control right there, O you who are preceded by the binding of salt.
Oṃ ciṭi ciṭi vikloli, bring such-and-such person together with his wealth and retinue, svāhā!
Having recited this ten thousand times according to the procedure for preliminary service, one then begins the actual practice (sādhana).

On his right and left sides, accompanied by the two goddesses Tārā and Bhṛkuṭī, one should visualize oneself as the Lord Āryāvalokiteśvara—red in color, adorned with garlands, garments, ornaments, and unguents, four-armed, holding a noose, a goad, a bow, and an arrow, characterized by the single aesthetic sentiment of *śṛṅgāra* (erotic passion), and standing beneath an Aśoka tree laden with flowers—at the three junctions of the day. One should then offer one hundred and eight oblations of salt. Within seven days, one brings under control either a man or a woman;
within twenty-one days, one brings even a great personage (*mahāpuruṣa*) into subjection.

Having fashioned an effigy of the person to be subjugated, measuring four finger-breadths in size, out of *madana* mixed with salt, one should heat it at the three junctions of the day over smokeless charcoal of *khadira* wood while reciting the mantra; by means of that person's name, they become subjugated.
Salt consecrated with *vajrodaka* and empowered by reciting the mantra one hundred and eight times should be given; by merely consuming it, one becomes subjugated. 53

Oṃ, you are salt-water, you are sharp, you are fierce, you are heart-piercing; the heart of so-and-so has been drunk; there is no physician in the world [who can cure it]. Oṃ ciṭi ciṭi, vikloli vikloli, mahāvikloli mahāvikloli, bring so-and-so under my control, svāhā!

Having performed the preliminary service (*pūrvasevā*) as before, he who drinks three handfuls of salt water at the three junctions of the day while reciting the name of another will bring that person under his control. Having made equal portions of salt and black mustard seeds, he who offers them in sacrifice while reciting the name of another will bring that person under his control.
Oṃ kurukulle svāhā.
This heart-mantra of the noble Āryatārā Bhaṭṭārikā possesses unimpeded power and is renowned for its efficacy in subjugating the three worlds.
Abiding in the previously mentioned samādhi, one should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times.
Afterwards, whoever is offered flowers, incense, ointments, powders, betel, and so forth, becomes submissive.
One should fumigate oneself with fragrant incense.
One becomes beloved by all people.
One should offer red flowers in a fire sacrifice while reciting the name of a person; that person will come under one's control.
Or, having consecrated food or drink with mantras, when it is consumed, that person will come under one's control.
For the subjugation of great beings (*mahāpuruṣavaśīkaraṇa*), white mustard seeds (*śvetasarṣapa*) are to be offered as oblations.

Subsequently, on an auspicious lunar day, asterism, and so forth, having performed worship of the Blessed Lady (*bhagavatī*), one should draw a sixteen-spoked wheel in the shape of a lotus petal upon birch bark or cloth using saffron, *gorocanā*, camphor, and other substances. In the center of the wheel, the name of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*) together with the mantra should be written.
On the petals, the name of the person to be accomplished should be written, constrained by the four syllables "Ku-Ru-Kul-le."

Outside, having encircled the wheel tripled with the syllable *oṃ* with a red thread and having inserted it into the center of the heart of a doll made of *madana* wood, one performs the attraction of the feet by heating it with charcoal from the *khadira* tree at the three junctions of the day.
For the subjugation of a man or a woman, having pierced the feet with a copper needle, one should heat it; [the target] becomes submissive.

Having visualized the wind mandala as fully perfected by means of the syllable *yaṃ*, one should contemplate the person to be acted upon (*sādhya*) situated above it—naked, with hair loose, bound at the neck with a noose, and seized at the heart with a hook. Having drawn him in by the force of the wind through the *vidyā* mantra and deposited him at the feet of the practitioner, one should perform everything [else].
Through practice, one can even effect the extraction of a physical body (*piṇḍākṛṣṭi*) by mere meditation.

By placing the mantra within clarified butter, honey, and sugar, worshipping it with flowers and other offerings at the three junctions of the day while reciting the mantra, one brings whoever one desires under control.

Having made a wick from the fibers of white lotuses and having produced soot in an unbaked clay bowl using the ghee of a tawny cow, one becomes beloved by all people when the eyes are anointed with that soot consecrated eight hundred times.

On the eighth or fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, at night in a cremation ground, one should prepare soot using a large skull and a wick made of white lotus fibers along with "great oil" (*mahātaila*).
When the eyes are anointed with that soot, one becomes beloved by all people. 55

O Amale, O Vimala, O Kuṅkuma! You are bound by the *samaya*. Drop by drop, by his will, the Lord rains, flashes, thunders, thunders; O Great King of Wonder, you who have arrived, you who increase [the joy], *huṃ*!

To the gods, to humans, to the *gandharvas*, O Lord of the *śikhigraha* deities, for the sake of the arrival of the seizer of bliss, for that which is to be approached and overcome, I sacrifice here, *svāhā*!

This is the procedure for the ritual service (*upacāra*) of the King of Mantras: having smeared the middle of the courtyard with cow dung and drawn the Goddess, one should spread *darbha* grass, kindle a fire, take eight hundred *arka* flowers, and while reciting the mantra, offer each flower individually into the fire.
One thereby attracts the desired woman or man. Knowing it to be effective, one should perform this task with skill and firm devotion. 56
Thus ends the fourth chapter in the *Siddhaikavīra-mahātantrarāja*;
thus the *Siddhaikavīra-mahātantrarāja* is completed.
